L6132: ## Reviewer's analysis:
L6133: ## - Study 20120277
L6134: (b) (6)
L6135: The sponsor's BE analysis excluded 6 subjects (Subjects
L6136: (b) (6)) using the criteria of "The PK parameter analysis set included subjects for
L6137: whom at least one of the PK parameters (AUCinf, AUClast, Cmax) could be adequately estimated for the purpose of primary analysis". The sponsor's analysis showed that the lower bound of 90% CI for AUCinf was 0.813. When the reviewer repeated the analysis in Phoenix 64, only two subjects need to be excluded (Subject [REDACTED](b) (6) due to protocol violation and Subject [REDACTED](b) (6) had %AUCinf extrapolated close to 50%). Reviewer's analysis showed that the lower bound of 90% CI for AUCinf was 0.799 and 90% CI for Cmax and AUClast both fall within the range of 0.8 to 1.25.
L6138: Although 0.799 barely missed the cutoff of 0.800, we consider that the PK comparability between the reference and test products in this study is established because 1) AUCinf was extrapolated and the extrapolation method may not be the most appropriate one for romosozumab, which has target mediated drug disposition and 2) The small difference in AUCinf is not expected to have any clinical implications.
L6139: - Study 20150197
Reviewer's analysis confirmed the sponsor's analysis. The PK comparability using BE criteria between the reference and test products in this study is established.
- Overall, we found the bridge between the to-be-marketed formulation (90 mg/mL [REDACTED](b) (4) PFS (Process 2 ARI) and clinical trial formulation (70 mg/mL glass PFS (Process 2 ATO) established based on data from the two PK comparability studies, Study 20120277 and 20150197.

L6182: ## 4.3.4. Study 20110227 (The Dedicated Renal Impairment Study)
L6183: Study 20110227 was an open-label, single-dose, parallel group Phase 1 Study of romosozumab in healthy subjects and subjects with Stage 4 renal impairment (RI) or Stage 5 renal impairment (ESRD) requiring hemodialysis. A total of 24 subjects (8 subjects with stage 4 RI, 8 subjects with ESRD requiring hemodialysis, and 8 healthy subjects) were enrolled in parallel into 1 of 3 treatment groups and each received a single 210 mg SC romosozumab dose.
L6184: The romosozumab concentration-time profiles by renal function group are shown in Figure 4.3.5. Descriptive statistics of PK parameter estimates by renal function group are presented in Table 4.3.7. A comparison of the PK parameters (tmax, Cmax, and AUC) between subjects with stage 4 RI (group 1), subjects with ESRD requiring hemodialysis (group 2), and healthy subjects (group 3) dosed at 210 mg SC are presented in Table 4.3.8 and Table 4.3.9. Individual PK parameters (Cmax and AUC) plot by group are presented in Figure 4.3.6.
L6185: Mean romosozumab exposure, as measured by Cmax and AUC values, in the stage 4 RI cohort was greater than the healthy cohort; mean Cmax and AUC were 29% and 44% higher in patients
L6186: with severe renal impairment as compared to healthy subjects. However, the exposure range in these two groups have substantial overlap. Most of the subjects with stage 4 RI had values that were within the range of healthy subjects, specifically, Cmax in 7 out of 8 subjects and AUC in 6 out of 8 subjects. In addition, mean romosozumab exposure was similar between subjects with ESRD requiring hemodialysis and healthy subjects.
L6187: The geometric least square mean point estimates and 90% CIs for the ratio of Cmax in subjects in stage 4 RI or subjects with ESRD requiring hemodialysis compared with healthy subjects were 1.313 (0.945, 1.824) (Table 4.2.8) and 0.895 (0.638, 1.256) (Table 4.3.9), respectively.
L6188: We note that, mechanistically speaking, it is unclear how the renal function/hemodialysis affects the exposure of romosozumab.
L6189: When it comes to safety, the most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse events in the dedicated RI study was hypocalcemia. Data suggested that the incidence of hypocalcemia was associated with severity of RI, but not with exposure of romosozumab. The number of subjects reported hypocalcemia was 0/8 in healthy subjects, 1/8 in subjects with severe RI, and 4/8 in subjects had ESRD requiring hemodialysis.

L6206: ## 4.3.5. Study 20060223 (Transitioning from Alendronate to Romosozumab Study)
L6207: Study 20060223 was a randomized, open-label, single-dose study in postmenopausal women with low bone mass who had been receiving alendronate for at least 1 year and in
L6208: postmenopausal women with low bone mass who were treatment-naïve for osteoporosis/bone loss. Subjects were to 1 of 3 groups as shown below.
L6209: - Group A: Subjects who had been receiving alendronate for at least 1 year and continued receiving alendronate (12 weekly dose of 70 mg alendronate or equivalent), beginning on day 1
- Group B: Subjects who had been receiving alendronate for at least 1 year and discontinued alendronate and received a single 3-mg/kg SC dose of romosozumab on day 1
- Group C: treatment-naïve subjects who received a single 3 mg/kg dose of romosozumab on day 1.
L6210: The romosozumab serum concentration-time profiles are shown in Figure 4.3.7. Descriptive statistics of PK parameter estimates by treatment group are presented in Table 4.3.10.
L6211: Mean Cmax values differed by less than 4% between groups B and C and median tmax values were similar (4.9 days and 4.5 days). The extents of exposure as measured by mean AUClast and AUCinf were also similar (&lt; 12% difference) and mean terminal half-life was approximately 7.5 days for both groups.

L6214: ## 4.3.6. Study 20060326 (The Dose-finding and Retreatment Study)
L6215: Study 20060326 was a randomized, placebo-controlled Phase 2 study to determine the effect of treatment with romosozumab versus placebo on lumbar spine BMD in postmenopausal women with low BMD. The study included a 24-month initial treatment phase during which subjects received romosozumab (419 subjects randomized to receive 70 mg, 140 mg, or 210 mg), placebo, or active control. Romosozumab and placebo were given QM or Q3M; one active control group received alendronate for the first 12 months followed by romosozumab for another 12 months, and the other active control group only received teriparatide 20 mcg QD for 12 months. Following initial treatment, subjects were re-randomized to a 12-month extension phase with denosumab or placebo; followed by a 12-month retreatment phase with romosozumab (the same dose regimen as in the initial treatment); followed by a 24-month follow-on phase with zoledronic acid or no intervention. Study design and treatment schema of Study 20060326 are shown in Figure 4.3.8 and 4.3.9.
L6216: Figure 4.3.8. Study Design and Treatment Schema_Study Day 1 to Month 24) (Source: Figure 8-1 of CSR Study 20060326)
L6217: Figure 4.3.9. Study Design and Treatment Schema_12-Month Denosumab Extension Phase and 12-Month Romosozumab Retreatment Phase) (Source: Figure 8-2 of CSR Study 20060326)
L6218: ALN = alendronate; AMG785 = romosozumab; EOS = end of study; PO = orally; QD = every day; QM
L6219: = every month; Q3M = every 3 months; Q6M = every 6 months; QW = every week; All subjects were to take at least 1000 mg elemental calcium and 800 IU vitamin D daily.
L6220: Note: Numbers in parentheses represented planned enrollment numbers, not actual. End of study is at 72 months.
L6221: Serum concentration-time profiles during 24-month romosozumab treatment phase followed by 12-Month Denosumab Extension Phase and a 12-Month Romosozumab Retreatment Phase are shown in Figure 4.3.10. Brief summaries of the PK results in each treatment phase is provided below.
L6222: ## - 24-month romosozumab treatment phase
L6223: For the QM cohorts, the peak serum romosozumab concentrations increased 3.7-fold after the first dose and 4.4-fold after the 12th dose for the 3-fold increase in dose from 70 to 210 mg. The peak concentration after the 12th dose ranged from 1.2- to 1.5-fold greater than the peak after the first dose for the 70, 140, and 210 mg QM doses.
L6224: Pharmacokinetic data for the QM cohorts were available before dosing, i.e., at trough concentration (Ctrough) time points at months 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, and 12 during the first year and ranged from 675 to 1070 ng/mL at the 70 mg QM dose, 2780 to 4770 ng/mL at the 140 mg QM dose, and 5640 to 9320 ng/mL at the 210 mg QM dose. During the second year, Ctrough data were collected at months 13, 14, 15, 18, 21, and 24, and ranged from 757 to 1120 ng/mL, 4880 to 6320 ng/mL, and 8310 to 10900 ng/mL, at the 70, 140, and 210 mg QM doses, respectively. Trough concentration values increased greater than dose proportionally. At Month 12 and Month 24, mean Ctrough at the 210 mg QM dose were 10-fold greater than concentrations at the 70 mg QM dose. Overall, the data indicate a greater extent of accumulation for 210 mg QM dosing than at 70 mg QM dosing.
L6225: For the Q3M cohorts, accumulation was minimal. The peak serum romosozumab concentrations increased 1.6-fold after the first dose and after the 12th dose for the 1.5-fold increase in dose from 140 to 210 mg. Mean romosozumab concentrations at trough time points for Q3M cohorts were below the quantitation limit (BQL).
L6226: The mean peak concentrations after the first dose of romosozumab at 140 mg QM for the cohort that received ALN treatment for the first year and for the cohort that received 24 months of romosozumab at 140 mg QM were similar at 12500 and 12400 ng/mL, respectively. Serum romosozumab Ctrough values ranged from 2590 to 5150 ng/mL for the ALN cohort and ranged from 2780 to 4770 ng/mL for the romosozumab 140 mg QM cohort. Mean Ctrough values after 12 doses of romosozumab at 140 mg in both groups were similar.
L6227: ## - Month 24 to 36 (denosumab extension) and month 36 to 48 (romosozumab retreatment)
L6228: After receiving denosumab or placebo during the third year of the study, subjects across all cohorts showed similar exposure during the retreatment phase regardless of their various treatments for the first 2 years.
L6229: For the cohort of subjects who received romosozumab treatment at 210 mg QM during the initial 2-year treatment followed by 12 months of denosumab prior to romosozumab retreatment, the average Ctrough values at steady state during the first 2 years of treatment (average concentration of the last 3 time points—months 18, 21, and 24) and average retreatment Ctrough at steady-state (average of concentrations at months 42, 45, and 48) were similar at 8940 ng/mL and 9420 ng/mL, respectively.
L6230: For the cohort that received romosozumab treatment at 210 mg QM during the initial 2-year treatment followed by 12 months of placebo prior to romosozumab retreatment, the average Ctrough values at steady state during the first 2 years and the average Ctrough at steady state during the retreatment phase were similar at 11300 ng/mL and 10900 ng/mL, respectively.
L6231: The average Ctrough value of the last 3 time points for the cohort that received placebo QM or Q3M during the initial 2-year treatment followed by 12 months of denosumab prior to romosozumab 210 mg QM in the retreatment period was 13900 ng/mL, 1.5-fold greater than the average Ctrough value over the last 3 time points of the first 2 years of romosozumab 210 mg treatment.
L6232: Figure 4.3.10. Mean Serum Romosozumab Concentration-time Profiles during 24-month romosozumab treatment phase followed by 12-Month Denosumab Extension Phase and a 12-Month Romosozumab Retreatment Phase (Source: Figure 11-2 of Study 20060326)
L6233: ## 4.3.7. Study 20101291 (The Dose Finding Study in Japanese Population)
L6234: Study 20101291 was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, multiple dose Phase 2 study in Japanese women with postmenopausal osteoporosis. Subjects received placebo or romosozumab 70 mg, 140 mg, or 210 mg by SC injection QM for 12 months.
L6235: The concentration-time profile of romosozumab is shown in Figure 4.3.11. Peak romosozumab concentrations increased 3.6-fold over the romosozumab 70 to 210 mg dose range (3-fold increase in dose). Mean serum concentrations measured 1 week after the administration of the first dose of romosozumab (day 8) were 7150, 16500, and 25600 ng/mL for the romosozumab 70, 140, and 210 mg groups, respectively. Trough serum romosozumab mean concentration values (from samples collected before dose administration at months 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, and 12) after multiple administrations with romosozumab ranged from 777 to 911 ng/mL, 3730 to 4590 ng/mL, and 6060 to 10400 ng/mL in the romosozumab 70, 140, and 210 mg groups, respectively. Trough concentrations demonstrated greater than dose proportional increases with ascending dose in the dose range of 70 mg to 210 mg, with the Month 12 time point exhibiting a 12-fold increase in concentration for a 3-fold increase in dose. Steady state was generally achieved by month 3 for all dose levels.
L6236: ## 4.3.8. Study 20070337 (The Pivotal Phase 3 Trial)
L6237: Study 20070337 was a multicenter, international, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel group study in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, to assess the effect of romosozumab treatment for 12 months compared with placebo on the incidence of vertebral and other fractures, and to assess the effect of romosozumab treatment for 12 months followed by
L6238: denosumab treatment for 12 months compared to placebo followed by denosumab treatment on the incidence of vertebral and other fractures (N = 7180).
L6239: Romosozumab PK were assessed in a PK substudy (931 subjects: romosozumab = 466, placebo = 465) to allow a PopPK analysis. Romosozumab serum concentrations were measured at day 1, day 14, month 1, month 3, month 3 + 14 days, month 6, month 6 + 14 days, month 9, month 12, and month 13.
L6240: After monthly administrations of romosozumab 210 mg to postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, exposure appeared to reach steady-state by month 3. Mean Ctrough from samples collected prior to dosing at months 3, 6, 9, and 12 ranged from 8050 to 9780 ng/mL. Two weeks after the fourth and seventh doses of romosozumab (month 3 plus 14 days and month 6 plus 14 days, respectively), peak concentrations were evaluated. Mean serum concentrations ranged from 21200 to 21900 ng/mL and were comparable after steady-state was reached.
L6241: Descriptive statistics of peak and trough serum romosozumab concentration-time data are shown in Table 4.3.11.

L6243: ## 4.4 Immunogenicity
L6244: ## 4.4.1. Immunogenicity incidences of ADA and NAb
L6245: In Phase 1 studies, about 7.9% (66 of 832) of subjects developed binding antibodies after at least 1 dose of romosozumab. All ADA positive subjects showed a persistent binding response with a positive result at the last time point tested. Neutralizing antibodies were detected in 2.1% (18 of 832) of all romosozumab dosed subjects, which is 27.3% (18/66) of all ADA+ subjects. See more detailed in Table 7 of Integrated Immunogenicity Report.
L6246: The incidence of anti-romosozumab binding antibodies in clinical studies with repeated dosing was higher than the antibody incidence following a single dose. About 20% (852 of 4289) of subjects exposed to romosozumab in the Phase 2 and 3 studies (Study 20070337, 20060326, 20101291, 20120156 and 20080289) developed binding antibodies. The antibody responses were transient (i.e., became negative by the last time point tested) for 9.7% (414 of 4289) of the overall dosed subjects. Neutralizing antibodies were detected in 1.1% (46 of 4289) of overall dosed subjects, 0.3% of which (11 of 4289) were transient. The percentage of ADA+ subjects who were NAb positive was 5.4% (46/852). See more detailed in Table 9 of Integrated Immunogenicity Report.
L6247: The incidence of binding and neutralizing antibodies in subject dosed with 210 mg QM was 19.1% (758 of 3959) and 0.8% (31 of 3959), respective. The percentage of ADA+ subjects who were NAb positive was 4.1% (31/758). This was similar to the incidences in the overall Phase 2 and 3 studies. See more detailed in Table 9 of Integrated Immunogenicity Report.
L6248: ## 4.4.2. Impact of ADA on PK
L6249: Overall, development of ADA was associated with reduced serum romosozumab concentrations.
L6250: ## 4.4.2.1 Impact of ADA on PK based on ADA+/ADA- status
L6251: In the Applicant's initial submission, the impact of immunogenicity on PK exposures was assessed by comparing romosozumab concentrations in subjects with anti-romosozumab antibodies to antibody-negative subjects in studies 20060326, 20101291 and 20070337.
L6252: In these 3 studies, romosozumab levels were reduced in some subjects with binding antibodies (approximately 25% lower exposure at months 3, 6, and/or 9 and comparable to each other with approximate 10% difference in mean values) at Month 12 (Table 4.4.1). Greater reduction in romosozumab levels at same time points were observed for subjects with neutralizing antibodies (Table 4.4.2).

L6265: ## 4.4.2.2 Impact of ADA on PK based on signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio
L6266: During the review cycle, the clinical pharmacology review team requested that the Applicant conduct further analysis regarding the relationship between titer and romosozumab concentration. The applicant did not have titer of immunogenicity samples and proposed to conduct the analysis between S/N ratio and romosozumab concentration. The new analysis was conducted based on data from Subject [REDACTED](b)(6) in Phase 1, the Phase 2 dose finding study (20060326), and the pivotal Phase 3 study (20070337). The scope of the analysis was decided for the following reasons: 1) Subject [REDACTED](b)(6) showed significant impact of immunogenicity on PK. 2) Study 20060326 had a retreatment period after subjects were off romosozumab for 12 months and, therefore, provided a good opportunity of investigating immunogenicity after retreatment. 3) The pivotal Phase 3 Study 20070337 enrolled 7180 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, which represents about 80% of the entire patient population in this submission. In general, the higher S/N ratio is, the lower the romosozumab exposure is.
L6267: Impact of immunogenicity on PK based on S/N ratio is summarized as follows:
L6268: - One of the neutralizing antibody positive subjects (Subject [REDACTED](b)(6)) from Phase 1 study 20060220 was inadvertently enrolled and dosed in a subsequent ascending multi-dose pharmacology/pharmacodynamic study 20060221. A rapid decline in romosozumab serum concentrations was observed in this subject after the first dose in study 20060221, and serum concentrations were not measurable after day 6, despite continued dosing once every two weeks (Figure 4.4.1).
L6269: **Figure 4.4.1 Serum Romosozumab Concentration (ng/mL) following 6 SC Q2W 1mg/kg doses (Subject [REDACTED](b)(6) in Study 20060221) (Source of data: Appendix Table 1.3-2 of CSR-20060221)**
L6270: Subject [REDACTED] (b) (6) had high signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio. Despite the interference from romosozumab in the sample, she was tested positive for neutralizing antibodies. Below is the narrative on this subject from the applicant,
L6271: Subject [REDACTED] (b) (6) received an initial single dose of romosozumab at 10 mg/kg subcutaneous (SC) on [REDACTED] (b) (6) in the romosozumab first-in-human Study 20060220. Of note, 10 mg/kg was the highest dose tested in the romosozumab clinical development program. On [REDACTED] (b) (6), a non-serious adverse event of injection site erythema was reported as mild in severity, related to study drug and resolved on [REDACTED] (b) (6) with no further action taken. The subject was positive for binding antibodies on [REDACTED] (b) (6) (study day 57; S/N value = 1.61) and for neutralizing antibodies on [REDACTED] (b) (6) (end of study [study day 85]; S/N value = 37.30). The subject returned for follow-up antibody testing as specified in the protocol. Prior to re-exposure of romosozumab in study 20060221, the subject's S/N values ranged from 382.05 to 1019.50. The subject was still positive for neutralizing antibodies when, in violation with the protocol in/exclusion criteria, she enrolled in romosozumab Study 20060221 (subject number [REDACTED] (b) (6)) and received a second dose of romosozumab at 1 mg/kg SC on [REDACTED] (b) (6) and then every 2 weeks until [REDACTED] (b) (6). At the time the subject was enrolled into Study 20060221, the investigator was not aware of her prior participation in the first-in-human study. The subject was tested for anti-romosozumab antibodies as per protocol, every month during Study 20060221 and approximately every 3 months after last dose: she remained positive for neutralizing antibodies as of [REDACTED] (b) (6) and was then lost to follow up. Throughout the study, the range of S/N for subject [REDACTED] (b) (6) was between 333.40 (before first dose) and 7,454.68; following the peak S/N value of 7,454.68 on study day 141, the values decreased over time to 639.83 at the subject's last follow-up visit.
L6272: - Among a total of 478 subjects enrolled in the PK substudy of 20070337, 95 subjects tested positive for anti-romosozumab binding antibodies at one or more time points post-baseline. Among the subjects with evaluable PK information, 9 subjects had S/N ratios &gt; 10 at Month 6 or 12, and their mean romosozumab serum concentrations were lower at these visits compared with the concentration values in subjects who tested negative for anti-romosozumab antibodies (Figure 4.4.2 and Figure 4.4.3)

L6275: ## 4.4.3. Impact of ADA on efficacy
L6276: Overall, ADA appeared to have no impact on efficacy. It is not feasible to draw a definitive conclusion on the impact of ADA on fracture, due to the small number of subjects who were ADA positive and fractured. There is lack of impact of ADA positive on BMD changes. Although the presence of ADA appeared to have a negative impact on bone turnover markers, the correlation between BTM and BMD, or between BTM and fracture is unclear.
L6277: ## 4.4.3.1 Impact of ADA on efficacy based on ADA+/ADA- status
L6278: In the Applicant's initial submission, the impact of immunogenicity on BMD was assessed by comparing romosozumab concentrations in subjects with anti-romosozumab antibodies to antibody-negative subjects in studies 20060326, 20101291 and 20070337. In each of these three studies, the effect of ADA on BMD change is similar for ADA positive and negative subjects. See Section 7 of Integrated Immunogenicity Report for more details.
L6279: ## 4.4.3.2 Impact of ADA on efficacy based on signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio
L6280: During the review cycle, we requested that the Applicant conduct further analysis regarding the relationship between titer and efficacy of romosozumab. The applicant did not have titer of immunogenicity samples and proposed to conduct the analysis between S/N ratio and efficacy of romosozumab. The scope of the new analysis is listed in Section 4.4.2.2 of this review.
L6281: The impacts of immunogenicity on efficacy based on S/N ratio are summarized below:
L6282: - Subjects experiencing a new vertebral fracture through Month 24 had an incidence of anti-romosozumab antibodies consistent with the overall patient population [4/21 (19.0%)]. The 4 subjects who tested positive for anti-romosozumab binding antibodies had S/N values ranging from 1.42 to 7.61 and tested negative for neutralizing antibodies.
- Analysis focused on the relationship between the immunoassay S/N values from Study 20070337 with percent change in BMD from baseline at months 12 and 24, showed no impact of the magnitude of the anti-romosozumab binding antibody response on BMD change from baseline across all anatomical sites and timepoints. Lumbar spine BMD data are listed as an example (Table 4.4.4).
- Consistent with those pharmacokinetic data shown in Figure 4.4.1, Subject (b)(6) had no notable changes in pharmacodynamic markers (ie, increases in P1NP and BMD) in Study 20060221.

L6286: ## 4.4.4 Impact of ADA on safety
L6287: Overall, ADA appeared to have no impact on safety. We defer to the clinical team regarding the impact of ADA on safety.
L6288: ## 4.4.4.1 Impact of ADA on safety based on ADA+/ADA- status
L6289: In the Applicant's initial submission, the impact of ADA on safety was based on data from the pivotal placebo-controlled Phase 3 study (20070337), with additional safety data coming from an active-controlled Phase 3 study with teriparatide (20080289), a dose-ranging placebo- and active-controlled (teriparatide or alendronate) study (20060326), a dose-ranging placebo-controlled study in Japanese women (20101291), and a placebo-controlled noninferiority study (20120156).
L6290: The following adverse events were evaluated for the timing of antibody onset and the corresponding antibody status: hypersensitivity, injection site reactions and autoimmune disorders. No associations could be made related to presence of anti-romosozumab binding and neutralizing antibodies and the worsening of immune mediated symptoms even after multiple dosing with romosozumab. Notable association was observed in the development of injection site reactions with romosozumab dosing when compared to placebo, however this was irrespective of the immunogenicity. See Table 14-8.3.7 of Module 5.3.5.3 – Integrated Summary of Safety for more details.
L6291: ## 4.4.4.2 Impact of ADA on safety based on signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio
L6292: In response to our information request described above, the Applicant further evaluated the impact of ADA on safety based on S/N ratio and safety data from Study 20070337. The pivotal Phase 3 Study 20070337 enrolled 7180 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, which represents about 80% of the entire patient population in this submission.
L6293: There were no notable differences in adverse reactions between subjects with S/N values &gt; 10 and placebo subjects, anti-romosozumab antibody negative subjects, or anti-romosozumab antibody positive subjects with S/N values ≤ 10 (Table 4.4.5). While the incidence of autoimmune disorders was slightly higher in the subset of antibody positive subjects with a S/N &gt; 10, this is likely due to the small size of this subset, as the 2 reported disorders (chronic gastritis and type IIa hyperlipidaemia) are unlikely to be a consequence of anti-drug antibodies.

L6303: ## 4.5 Population PK Analyses
L6304: The population PK review is comprised of two parts: first part is the Applicant's analysis (Section 4.5.1) and the second part is the Reviewer's comments and analysis (Section 4.5.2).
L6305: ## 4.5.1 Applicant's analysis
L6306: A population PK analysis was conducted by the Applicant to characterize the pharmacokinetics of romosozumab administered IV or SC in healthy subjects and postmenopausal women with low BMD or osteoporosis. The clinically relevant covariates which may explain the variability of the PK parameters were explored and the individual exposure estimates were computed for the subsequent exposure-response analyses.
L6307: Overall, 11 clinical studies were pooled for population PK analysis including 8 Phase 1 studies (20060220, 20060221, 20060223, 20090378, 20101180, 20120277, 20110227, and 20110253), 2 Phase 2 studies (20060326 and 20101291), and 1 pivotal Phase 3 studies (20070337). In these studies, romosozumab was administered as a single IV dose (N=12 subjects) of 1 mg/kg or 5 mg/kg; a single SC dose (N=359 subjects) of 0.1 mg/kg to 10 mg/kg or 210 mg; or as multiple SC doses (N=1098 subjects) ranging from 1 to 3 mg/kg given every 2 or 4 weeks or fixed doses of 70, 140, or 210 mg given every month or 3 months for up to 48 months.
L6308: A nonlinear mixed effect modeling approach was implemented to characterize the population PK of romosozumab using NONMEM 7.2. A three-compartment PK model with linear distribution to peripheral compartments and parallel linear elimination in the central compartment and target-mediated non-linear elimination in the peripheral compartments was selected as the structural model. A saturable FcRn-mediated absorption process was used to describe romosozumab absorption and bioavailability after SC administration. The model schematic and parameters are shown in Figure 1.
L6309: **Figure 1 Model Schematic for Romosozumab PKPD**
L6310: Source: Applicant's population PK report, Figure 13-12, Page 96.
L6311: The covariates considered for the analysis were demographic factors, including sex, age, race (Japanese vs non-Japanese), body weight; renal function estimated using the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease (MDRD) formula, prior alendronate administration, and drug product manufacturing process (1: clinical process; 2: commercial process). The summary statistics of covariates by study were listed in Table 1. The final dataset contained 13346 serum concentrations of romosozumab from 1459 subjects, including 341 (138 male, 203 female) healthy subjects, 35 (12 male, 23 female) with low BMD, and 419 osteopenic or 664 osteoporotic postmenopausal women. The median body weight was 61 kg and ranged from 33 to 109 kg. The overall median age was 66 years and ranged from 20 to 89 years. The median eGFR was 80 mL/min/1.73 m2 and ranged from 7 to 144 mL/min/1.73 m2. The majority of subjects were Caucasian (51%), 14% Japanese, 7% Hispanic, 4% Black, and rest from other races.

L6335: ## 1. Impact of covariates on romosozumab exposure
L6336: The impact of other covariates, in addition to body weight, on steady-state romosozumab exposure parameters (AUCss and Cmax,ss) after a clinical dose of 210 mg SC QM is shown using a forest plot (Figure 5).
L6337: Figure 5 Fold Change and 95%PI in Steady-state AUC and Cmax across the Range of Covariates:
L6338: Vertical reference lines refer to 0.8, 1.0 and 1.25 fold-changes in median model predicted AUC and Cmax at steady state, compared to the reference subject. Renal function based on eGFR: normal (\ge 90 mL/min/1.73 m^2), mild (60 to &lt;90 mL/min/1.73 m^2), moderate (30 to &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m^2), severe (15 to &lt;30 mL/min/1.73 m^2), ESRD (5 to &lt;15 mL/min/1.73 m^2).

L6340: The reference subject is a subject with weight of 61 kg, age of 66 years, mild renal function, male, race of non-Japanese, and using the formulation utilized in the clinical studies. Although these covariates have significant associations with romosozumab PK parameters, the distributions of romosozumab AUCss and Cmax,ss fold change with respect to the reference subject overlapped greatly across covariate ranges, suggesting their impact on overall PK variability is small and resulted in less than 20% difference in exposure for most covariates. Body weight and advanced renal impairment (severe renal impairment and ESRD without hemodialysis) showed PK changes beyond the empirically defined region of clinical importance (0.8 - 1.25).
L6341: ## 2. Justification of a non-weight Based Dosing for Clinical use in PMO Patients

L6351: To conclude, prior alendronate or PMO treatments, patient populations (eg, healthy/low-BMD, osteopenic, and osteoporotic), antibody status (eg, negative, binding vs. neutralizing), and baseline sclerostin had no significant association with romosozumab PK parameters. Therefore, these covariates had no impact on romosozumab exposures and no dose adjustments are proposed based on these factors. Body weight and renal function (as measured by eGFR) were significant covariates with increasing exposure predicted for decreasing body weight or eGFR. Considering the fixed dosing regimen was given to Phase 3 study with an acceptable safety profile, dose adjustment based on body weight or renal function is not warranted.
L6352: ## 4.5.2 Reviewer's comments:
L6353: The reviewer found the Applicant's population PK model structure for romosozumab reasonable. The applicant's population PK dataset included ESRD patients with hemodialysis from study 20110227 (the dedicated renal impairment study) When the reviewer reran the population PK analysis, these patients were removed for the following reasons.
L6354: - Data from the dedicated renal impairment study showed that the exposure in severe renal impairment subjects was 44% higher than that in subject with normal renal function, whereas the exposure in ESRD subjects with hemodialysis was comparable to that in subjects with normal function (Table 4). The reason behind the scene is unknown as hemodialysis does hardly remove large molecules. In the dedicated renal impairment study, PK samples were intensively collected over 85 days after a single dose of 210 mg. When hemodialysis occurred on a day of sample collection, sample collections were performed before hemodialysis. The frequency of hemodialysis in ESRD patients was not specified. It appears that the impact of hemodialysis on PK of romosozumab is inconclusive.

L6417: Initial modeling was performed using the mechanistic PK/PD model developed to describe the on-treatment PD efficacy (BMD) effects of romosozumab using the 24-month initial treatment phase Study 60326 and 12-month Study 1291 data. Individual romosozumab PK parameter estimates for PK/PD modeling were derived in population PK analysis (section 4.5). The effects of study (1291 vs. 60326) on baseline BMD were included in the base model. The base model also included an effect of DXA (hologic vs. lunar) machine type on baseline BMD.
L6418: In the final model, the body weight and PMO were added to the population PK/PD model. Diagnostic plots revealed that the model was consistent with the observed data and little systematic bias was evident (Figure 9). The VPC results revealed that the full model for two-year efficacy provided a reliable description of the data with adequate precision of structural model and variance parameter estimates (Figure 10). Parameter estimates are listed in Table 11. The population mean estimate for \logit(I_{max} \times) was -0.812 (67.0%), corresponding to an I_{max} value of 0.307. Estimates for IC_{50} and SC_{50} were 70.4 ng/mL and 22,600 ng/mL. Differences in baseline BMD for study 1291 subjects (approximately 15% lower) and lunar machine measurements (15% higher) were identified.

L6428: Once a suitable population PK/PD model was developed, an extension to the base model was developed to describe the on-treatment, off-treatment and re-treatment PD efficacy (BMD) effects of romosozumab using only Study 60326 data that included the off-treatment (nominal months 24-36) and romosozumab re-treatment. Additional model development was driven by deviances between the model-predicted and observed markers for the off-treatment and re-treatment periods. The final model was updated by adding a rebound and rebound precursor pool with the precursor affecting the resorption cavity input. VPC results for the re-treatment model are presented in Figure 11. These VPC plots were stratified by the romosozumab dose regimen that was administered prior to the off-treatment period. Results were presented for the entire study period (0-48 months), the off-treatment phase only (24-36 months), and the re-treatment phase only (36-48 months).
L6429: To conclude, the two-year efficacy of romosozumab was described by exposure-BMD model. The model provides a reasonable representation of the effects of romosozumab on BMD.

L6439: The results indicate that the BMD is comparable across renal function categories. The similar conclusion can be drawn based on the primary efficacy endpoint, new vertebral fracture. There is no trend that the BMD %CFB and/or new vertebral fracture rate would be increased in more severe renal impairment patients. On the other side, BMD %CFB was decreased around 37% and 34% for 12 and 24 month in highest body weight group compared to that in lowest body weight group. However, this difference did not result in any clinically significant differences in incident rates of new vertebral fracture across body weight range. All these results demonstrate that no dose adjustment is necessary based on body weight and renal function from efficacy perspective.
L6440: From safety perspective, only one subject with hypocalcemia was identified in the Phase 3 study. In the dedicated renal impairment study (Study 20110227), hypocalcemia were reported to 5 subjects, 1 severe renal impairment subject and 4 ESRD subjects with hemodialysis. Based on Table 4 in section 4.5, the exposure in ESRD subjects with hemodialysis was comparable to that in normal renal function subject. Thus, the higher event rate of hypocalcemia is not driven by the exposure, which further support that no dose adjustment is necessary based on renal function.

L6470: DUKE Clinical Research Institute (DCRI)
Prospectively defined process for pivotal phase 3 studies
Focus of review was SAEs only
Events for adjudication identified mostly by prespecified lists of "trigger" terms
Outcome options of positive and negative
Negative adjudication included events with insufficient documentation
Flowchart (DCRI):
All clinical trial adverse events split into SAEs and Non-SEAs (STOP).
SAEs split into Amgen-identified potential CV SAEs (prespecified lists of trigger terms) and Investigator-identified potential CV SAEs.
Amgen-identified potential CV SAEs and Investigator-identified potential CV SAEs both feed into DCRI-identified potential CV SAEs.
DCRI-identified potential CV SAEs split into Suspected CV SAEs sent for adjudication and SAEs not meeting criteria for adjudication (STOP).
Suspected CV SAEs sent for adjudication split into Adjudicated positive and Adjudicated negative.
Adjudicated positive and Adjudicated negative both lead to True negative.
Adjudicated negative also leads to Insufficient Documentation.
Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) Study Group
Additional posthoc evaluation of pivotal phase 3 studies
Events identified for adjudication by independent medical review of all adverse events (SAEs and non-SEAs), narratives for SAEs, concomitant medications, general comments, and cardiac imaging
Outcome options of positive, negative, and suspected
Suspected category included events with insufficient documentation
Flowchart (TIMI):
All clinical trial adverse events split into SAEs and Non-SEAs.
SAEs and Non-SEAs both feed into Medical/safety review.
Medical/safety review splits into Potential CV events sent for adjudication and Non-suspected events (STOP).
Potential CV events sent for adjudication splits into Adjudicated positive, Adjudicated negative, and Adjudicated suspected.
Non-suspected events also leads to Adjudicated suspected.
Controlled by DCRI (left side) and Controlled by TIMI (right side).

L6519: Diagram illustrating the mechanism of action for Romosozumab. The left panel shows the normal bone remodeling cycle where Sclerostin inhibits Osteoblasts and Osteoprogenitors, leading to bone resorption by Osteoclasts. The right panel shows Romosozumab binding to Sclerostin, inhibiting its action, leading to increased Osteoblast activity, increased New Bone Matrix formation, and recruitment of Osteoprogenitors, resulting in increased bone formation and decreased bone resorption.

L6526: Figure 7 is a schematic diagram illustrating the Study 20070326 design. The study is divided into three main phases: M24/RANDOMIZATION/EXTENSION, M36/RE-TREATMENT, and M48/EARLY TERMINATION/M51/EOS.
The timeline starts at Month 0 and extends to Month 47 (Q6M visits).
M24/RANDOMIZATION/EXTENSION (Months 0 to 24):
Subjects are randomized into five groups based on AMG 785 dosing regimen (70 mg, 140 mg, or 210 mg SC QM) or placebo (SC QM).
Subjects in the AMG 785 groups are further randomized 1:1 to receive either AMG 785 or placebo for the next 12 months (M24 to M36).
Subjects in the placebo group are randomized 1:1 to receive either AMG 785 or placebo for the next 12 months (M24 to M36).
Subjects in the ALN 70 mg PO QW group are randomized 1:1 to receive either AMG 785 140 mg SC QM or placebo for the next 12 months (M24 to M36).
M36/RE-TREATMENT (Months 24 to 36):
Subjects in the AMG 785 groups receive AMG 785 210 mg SC QM.
Subjects in the placebo group receive placebo SC Q6M.
M48/EARLY TERMINATION/M51/EOS (Months 36 to 47):
Subjects in the AMG 785 groups receive AMG 785 210 mg SC QM.
Subjects in the placebo group receive placebo SC Q6M.

L6541: Figure 1 illustrates the effects of Sclerostin and Romosozumab on Canonical Wnt Signaling and Bone Formation and Resorption.
A: Sclerostin Inhibition of Canonical Wnt Signaling
An Osteocyte secretes Sclerostin. Sclerostin binds to LRP5/6 coreceptors, preventing Wnt ligand engagement. This inhibits the formation of the Wnt/LRP5/6/Frizzled complex. Consequently, Axin is not phosphorylated, GSK-3\beta remains active, leading to proteasomal degradation of \beta-catenin in the cytoplasm. \beta-catenin levels decrease, resulting in no gene transcription in the nucleus and decreased bone formation.
B: Romosozumab Reversal of Sclerostin Inhibition
Romosozumab, a monoclonal antibody, binds to Sclerostin, blocking its interaction with LRP5/6 coreceptors. This allows Wnt ligands to engage LRP5/6/Frizzled, activating Canonical Wnt signaling. Axin is phosphorylated, GSK-3\beta is inhibited, and \beta-catenin accumulates in the cytoplasm and translocates to the nucleus. This leads to gene transcription and increased bone formation.
L6542: Figure 1 illustrates the activation of Wnt/\beta-catenin signaling in osteoblasts/osteoblast precursors and its anabolic effect on bone.
A: Precursor/osteoblast
Wnt/\beta-catenin signaling leads to increased OPG production (\uparrowOpg) and decreased Rankl/Opg ratio (\downarrowRankl/Opg), resulting in reduced osteoclast formation and increased bone mass.
B: Osteocyte
Wnt/\beta-catenin signaling in osteocytes increases OPG (\uparrowOpg) and Rankl (\uparrowRankl) production. Sost/sclerostin production is also increased (\uparrowSost/sclerostin). The increased Rankl/Opg ratio (\uparrowRankl/Opg) leads to increased osteoclast formation and osteoblast production, resulting in a positive balance and bone gain.
C: All osteoblastic cells
Anti-sclerostin treatment neutralizes sclerostin, leading to increased Wnt/\beta-catenin signaling in all osteoblastic cells. This results in increased OPG production and decreased Rankl/Opg ratio, leading to increased osteoclast formation and osteoblast production, resulting in increased bone formation.

L6544: This diagram shows the positive bone balance in remodeling sites in vertebra of monkeys treated with (A) vehicle or (B) 30mg/kg AMG785. Bone balance in BRU is shown in (C).

Solid lines outline the resorption and formation phases of the bone remodeling cycle, with the dashed lines representing the thickness of osteoid overlaying mineralized bone. Colored and white lines represent lamellae with a thickness of 3.2 µm. Bone balance, representing the difference between resorption depth and final W.Th, was negative in the vehicle control group (blue) and positive in the romosozumab (purple) group. Data are mean ± SEM. *P < 0.05 vs vehicle by t-test. n = 9/group.
Conclusions	Romosozumab increased wall thickness and decreased final resorption depth, yielding a positive bone balance that probably contributes to the increased bone volume and mass. RsP+RvP were decreased and FP increased which explains reduction in eroded surface at trabecular surfaces.
Reviewer Comments	
Study provided detailed information on the dynamic events in a bone remodeling unit (BRU) in monkey vertebra, specifying the MOA of anti-Scl Ab AMG785 at the tissue level.
Sponsor did not distinguish resorption from reversal period, and the calculated 'resorption period' was in fact the combination of resorption and reversal periods. According to Reviewer's analysis of histomorphometry data from Study 107903 (cancellous ilium at 13 wks, and femoral neck at 12 months), AMG785 caused a larger reduction in reversal ("resting") period than in resorption period.
The positive bone balance in the bone remodeling unit may also be achieved during modeling-based bone formation (MBF) at the various bone surfaces

Figure showing bone remodeling cycle diagrams for Vehicle (A) and Romosozumab (B) groups, and Bone Balance (C).

L6546: Diagram illustrating the potential mechanism of action of Scl-Ab with acute and chronic administration, showing gene network changes in osteocytes.
Acute Phase
Scl-Ab inhibits Wnt Inhibitors (Sost). This leads to activation of Tcf/Lef Wnt signaling. Tcf/Lef Wnt signaling activates OPG, Wisp1, Twist1, Bglap, and c-Myc. OPG and Wisp1 lead to Osteoclast Activity Decrease. Twist1, Bglap, and c-Myc lead to Bone Formation Increase (Lining cell activation, OB vigor \uparrow, OP recruitment \uparrow).
Chronic Phase
Scl-Ab inhibits Wnt Inhibitors (DKK1, Sost, Wnt5b). This leads to activation of Tcf/Lef Wnt signaling. Tcf/Lef Wnt signaling activates OPG, Wisp1, and c-Myc. OPG and Wisp1 lead to Osteoclast Activity Decrease. Tcf/Lef Wnt signaling also activates p53 (annotated with a star). p53 activates Dmp1 and Twist1. Dmp1 activates Cdkn2a (p14/ARF). Cdkn2a activates RB1. RB1 activates p21. p21 activates p53 (negative feedback loop). p53 and p21 lead to Bone Formation Self-Regulation (OP recruitment \downarrow, MS/BS & MAR normalize). p53 also inhibits c-Myc. c-Myc is inhibited by p53 and p21. c-Myc is also inhibited by Csfl.

AMG 785 treatment significantly increases Trabecular BMD compared to OVX control (*p<0.05). A significant linear dose effect is observed (\lambda<0.05), with higher doses (30 mg/kg) showing greater increases than lower doses (3 mg/kg). A significant quadratic dose effect is also observed (\phi<0.05), suggesting a non-linear relationship between dose and BMD increase.

L6593: Figure 2 is a semi-log plot showing Serum AMG 785 Concentration (ng/mL) on the Y-axis (log scale, ranging from 1 to 100,000) versus Time (hr) on the X-axis (linear scale, ranging from 0 to 504). The plot compares the mean (\pmSD) concentration-time profiles for AMG 785 administered as 3 mg/kg FIH (N=9, solid line with black circles) or 2.75 mg/kg CPD (N=10, dashed line with white circles).
Both groups show rapid absorption, reaching peak concentrations around 48 hours. The FIH group generally maintains slightly higher concentrations than the CPD group during the initial phase (up to 168 hours). The FIH group shows a slower decline in concentration compared to the CPD group after 252 hours.

L6624: Figure 1: Model Schematic for Romosozumab PKPD. The diagram illustrates a three-compartment pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PKPD) model. The central compartment (Central, V2) receives input from IV dose (DoseIV) and SC dose (DoseSC) via the Absorption Site. The SC dose is absorbed into the FcRn-Ab compartment (Absorption Site) via KSS, FcRn. The FcRn-Ab compartment is also connected to the Unbound Ab compartment (Unbound Ab) via Kdeg. The Unbound Ab compartment is connected to the Central compartment via k1. The Central compartment is connected to Peripheral 1 (Periph1, V3) via Q3 and to Peripheral 2 (Periph2, V4) via Q4. Peripheral 1 and Peripheral 2 are connected to their respective Scavenging (Scl) compartments (Scl Periph1 and Scl Periph2) via KSS. The Scl compartments are connected to the Complex compartments (Complex Periph1 and Complex Periph2) via Kint. The Complex compartments are connected back to the Scl compartments via Kint. The Scl compartments are also connected to the Central compartment via CL.
